titleStmt.title: Telegram From the Embassy in Venezuela to the Department of State

div.head: 476. Telegram From the Embassy in Venezuela to the Department of State
div.p: 3921. Subject: President Reagan’s telecon with President Lusinchi of Venezuela of April 4, 1984.

2. During President Reagan’s call to President Lusinchi, thanking him for Venezuela’s assistance with the Argentine debt package, President Lusinchi indicated that he had some thoughts on the overall Latin American debt crisis, and that he would convey them through me. Subsequently, President Lusinchi and I discussed this matter. Today he sent me a note on the subject through the Minister of Finance. A translation of the note is as follows:

3. Quote. The Government of Venezuela is very concerned about the increase in interest rates in the United States and the existence of expectations of further increases in the near future, which make extremely onerous the servicing of debt contracted with the international banks by Latin American countries. In some cases it may make it impossible to fulfill the obligations contracted. For the stability of the international financial system, and the recovery of the economy of these countries, it would be advisable to have preferential fixed interest rates established in agreements which are entered into for refinancing the debt. End quote.

note.p: Source: Department of State, Central Foreign Policy File, Electronic Telegrams, D840292–0585. Confidential; Immediate. Also sent Immediate to the White House and the Department of the Treasury.

In a May 9 memorandum to McFarlane, Burghardt and Menges noted: “Venezuela has $35 billion in outstanding debt. The public sector portion—$27 billion—is up to date, but the private sector portion is $800–900 million in arrears. The GOV has decided that it will not enter into an IMF agreement or Paris Club arrangement and, instead, will unilaterally reschedule the private debt—a very unusual approach. Treasury is particularly concerned about how some $200 million in ExIm Bank claims will be covered and has threatened negative actions. But there appears to be general agreement (even in Treasury) to avoid punitive measures as long as the GOV demonstrates its seriousness in dealing with the debt problem. The Lusinchi government is a marked improvement over its predecessor on this score.” (Reagan Library, Executive Secretariat, NSC Country File, Latin America/Central, Venezuela (02/03/1984–12/17/1984))
